title: Evaluation from the walking-isomorphism cotensor is a Dwyer--Kan equivalence
statement:
Use small simplicial sets, Kan complexes, homotopy fibers and weak homotopy equivalences from [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], the Kan model structure of [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper], and the Reedy model structure of [lem-coef-reedy-model-structure]. A simplicial space is a functor $V:\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathrm{sSet}$. It is a Segal space if it is Reedy fibrant and its consecutive-edge maps $V_n\to V_1\times_{V_0}\cdots\times_{V_0}V_1$ are weak homotopy equivalences for every $n\geq2$. For vertices $x,y$ of $V_0$, let $M_V(x,y)$ be the strict fiber of $(d_1,d_0):V_1\to V_0^2$. The homotopy category $hV$ has those vertices as objects, morphisms $\pi_0M_V(x,y)$, identity from $s_0$, and composition from the degree-two Segal map and $d_1$.

For $n\geq0$ let $F(n)_k=\operatorname{Hom}_\Delta([k],[n])$, discrete in the inner direction, and let $cK$ be the constant simplicial space on a simplicial set $K$. For simplicial spaces $A,V$, use the cartesian internal hom of [lem-coef-segal-cartesian-exponent], explicitly $$(V^A)_{n,q}=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{sS}}(A\times F(n)\times c\Delta^q,V),$$ with operators given by precomposition. Let $I[1]$ be the groupoid with objects $0,1$ and exactly one morphism between each ordered pair, let $E$ be its nerve discrete in the inner direction, and let $e_i:F(0)\to E$ select $i$, for $i=0,1$. For a Segal space $W$, put $p_i=W^{e_i}:W^E\to W$ and let $j:W\to W^E$ be induced by $E\to F(0)$. The simplicial space $W^E$ is a Segal space. Call a map $t:A\to B$ of Segal spaces a Dwyer--Kan equivalence if $ht:hA\to hB$ is an equivalence of ordinary categories and $M_A(x,y)\to M_B(tx,ty)$ is a weak homotopy equivalence for every pair of vertices $x,y$ of $A_0$.

For every Segal space $W$, the constant-diagram map $j:W\to W^E$ and both evaluation maps $p_0,p_1:W^E\to W$ are Dwyer--Kan equivalences. No completeness assumption on $W$ is imposed.

source.place: Lemma 13.9, printed pp. 31-32, with Sections 2.3, 4-5, 7.4 and Corollary 7.3 for the conventions. Read online 2026-10-17; not archived in literature/. No Stacks tag states this Segal-space theorem.

proof.text: Put $A=W^E$ and $B=W^{F(1)}$, and let $a:F(1)\hookrightarrow E$ select $0\to1$. The exponent lemma makes $A,B$, and each $W^{F(n)}$, Segal spaces. Write $r=W^a:A\to B$ and $s=rj:W\to B$, where $s$ is induced by $F(1)\to F(0)$. All these maps commute with the outer endpoint operators. The inclusions $\partial F(1)\hookrightarrow F(1)$ and any union of edges $K\hookrightarrow F(2)$ give Kan fibrations on mapping spaces into $W$, by taking degree zero in the restriction clause of the exponent lemma. In particular the endpoint maps of $W,A,B$ are Kan fibrations, so their strict mapping fibers represent homotopy fibers. All spaces here are small Kan complexes, by Reedy fibrancy.

source.place: Lemma 13.9, the diagram on p.31; Corollary 7.3 and Sections 2.3-2.5.

proof.text: We first prove that $hj$ is an equivalence of ordinary categories, without using Proposition 13.8. For $i=0,1$, define a functor $h_i:I[1]\times I[1]\to I[1]$ by $h_i(u,0)=i$ and $h_i(u,1)=u$. Every object function into this groupoid extends uniquely to a functor. Its nerve is a map $E\times E\to E$: degreewise it applies $h_i$ to the paired strings of vertices. Currying evaluation after this map gives $H_i:A\times E\to A$, with endpoint restrictions $jp_i$ and $1_A$, while $p_i j=1_W$ strictly. For any Segal space $U$, the product $U\times E$ is again a Segal space: $E$ is Reedy fibrant, since its matching maps are maps of discrete simplicial sets and every horn in a discrete simplicial set is constant, so such maps are Kan fibrations; Reedy fibrations are characterized by matching maps, and these maps for $U\times E$ are the products of those for $U$ and $E$; finally the Segal maps of $U\times E$ are products of those of $U$ with the Segal bijections of the nerve $E$. The mapping fiber of $U\times E$ from $(x,k)$ to $(y,l)$ is $M_U(x,y)$ times the one-point set consisting of the unique arrow $k\to l$; identities and degree-two compositions are coordinatewise. Thus $h(U\times E)=hU\times I[1]$. Applying this to $H_i$ gives a natural isomorphism $h(jp_i)\cong1_{hA}$: its component at $b$ is the class of $H_i(s_0b,0\to1)$, its inverse is the reverse arrow, and functoriality on the two triangles expressing a square proves naturality. Together with $h(p_i j)=1_{hW}$, this makes $hj$ and $hp_i$ quasi-inverse functors.

source.place: First paragraph of Proposition 13.8, used in Lemma 13.9; Proposition 13.5, with the contraction written explicitly.

proof.text: The classifier applied to $V=W^{F(n)}$ identifies $r_n:A_n\to B_n$ with the weak equivalence $(V^E)_0\to V_{\mathrm{eq}}$ followed by inclusion $V_{\mathrm{eq}}\subseteq V_1$. The identification is currying and interchange of the factors $E,F(n)$; it respects the actual endpoint maps. Consequently every homotopy fiber of $r_n$ is either empty or contractible: over a component outside $V_{\mathrm{eq}}$ there is no path into the image, and over a component inside it the homotopy fiber is that of the classifier weak equivalence. The contractible-fiber criterion justifies the latter assertion. The same holds for $r_0\times r_0$, since its homotopy fibers are the products of the two respective homotopy fibers.

source.place: Lemma 13.9, application of Theorem 6.2 to W^{F(n)}; homotopy monomorphisms as in Section 12.2.

proof.text: The square of simplicial sets $\Delta^1\times\Delta^1$ is the union of its two nondegenerate triangles along their common diagonal. More explicitly those triangles have vertices $((0,0),(1,0),(1,1))$ and $((0,0),(0,1),(1,1))$; every weakly increasing string in the square lies in one of them and their intersection is the diagonal. After taking discrete outer nerves and mapping into $W$, this gives the strict identification $B_1=W_2\times_{W_1,d_1,d_1}W_2$, with endpoint map $(d_2\pi_1,d_0\pi_2):B_1\to B_0^2=W_1^2$. The map $s_1:W_1\to B_1$ is $(s_0,s_1)$ and $s_0:W_0\to B_0$ is the degeneracy $s_0$. The simplicial identities show that all four maps form the large rectangle of Lemma 13.9. The notation $s_n$ here denotes degree $n$ of the map $s$; the degeneracies in the displayed pairs are the ordinary degeneracies of $W$.

source.place: Lemma 13.9, second displayed square on pp.31-32; explicit two-triangle decomposition.

proof.text: Here is the missing computation for that rectangle. Let $L=\{(x,\sigma)\in W_0\times W_2:d_2\sigma=s_0x\}$ and $R=\{(\tau,y)\in W_2\times W_0:d_0\tau=s_0y\}$. The degree-two Segal map $(d_2,d_0):W_2\to W_1\times_{W_0}W_1$ is also a Kan fibration by restriction to the two consecutive edges, hence a trivial Kan fibration. Pulling it back with the first edge an identity gives a trivial fibration $L\to W_1$, $(x,\sigma)\mapsto d_0\sigma$, and with the second edge an identity gives a trivial fibration $R\to W_1$, $(\tau,y)\mapsto d_2\tau$. Their sections are $f\mapsto(d_1f,s_0f)$ and $f\mapsto(s_1f,d_0f)$, so these sections are weak equivalences. Instead use $d_1:L\to W_1$ and $d_1:R\to W_1$: they are Kan fibrations by restriction to the edge pairs $(d_2,d_1)$ and $(d_1,d_0)$, respectively, followed by the same identity-edge pullback. Each has the same section, and its composite with that section is the identity. Two-out-of-three for weak homotopy equivalences therefore makes both $d_1$ maps trivial fibrations. These applications require no completeness. Pullbacks and composites of trivial fibrations are trivial fibrations: a boundary lifting problem is solved in the original map, or successively in the two maps. Thus $L\times_{W_1,d_1,d_1}R\to W_1$ is a trivial fibration. It is over $W_0^2$, with the map to $W_1$ giving the common diagonal. For fixed $x,y$, its restriction is a trivial fibration $M_B(s_0x,s_0y)\to M_W(x,y)$ whose section is the map induced by $s$. Hence $M_W(x,y)\to M_B(s_0x,s_0y)$ is a weak equivalence.

source.place: Lemma 13.9, computation using Lemma 12.4; degree-two Segal maps and identity-edge pullbacks, with the computation expanded.

proof.text: Fix $x,y\in W_0$ and write $J:M_W(x,y)\to M_A(jx,jy)$ and $T:M_A(jx,jy)\to M_B(s_0x,s_0y)$ for the maps induced by $j,r$. Put $b=(jx,jy)$ and $c=(s_0x,s_0y)$. For $n=0,1$, use exactly the classifier factorization of step 3: after currying, $C_n=(W^{F(n)})_{\mathrm{eq}}\subseteq B_n$ and $r_n':A_n\to C_n$ is a weak equivalence. Write $\partial=(d_1,d_0)$. The map $\partial_B$ sends $C_1$ into $C_0^2$: each component of $C_1$ meets $r_1'(A_1)$, its endpoint there is in $C_0^2$ by commutation with $r$, and a simplicial map sends each component into one component. Apply [lem-coef-kan-component-restriction-fibration] to $\partial_B:B_1\to B_0^2$, a Kan fibration by step 1. It gives a Kan fibration $\partial_C:C_1\to C_0^2$ whose fiber over $c$ is $D=M_B(s_0x,s_0y)\cap C_1$, a union of components of $M_B(s_0x,s_0y)$. It also makes $C_0,C_1$ Kan.

source.place: Lemma 13.9, printed p. 31: 'i* is a homotopy monomorphism ... whence j* is a weak equivalence'; homotopy monomorphism in the sense of Section 12.2 (weak equivalence onto a union of components), expanded through the fiberwise Kan-fibration criterion.

proof.text: The map $v=r_0'\times r_0':A_0^2\to C_0^2$ is a weak equivalence by [lem-coef-kan-pullback-fibration-invariance]. Explicitly apply that statement to the cospans $A_0\to\Delta^0\leftarrow A_0$ and $C_0\to\Delta^0\leftarrow C_0$, with comparison maps $r_0',1_{\Delta^0},r_0'$. The first legs are Kan fibrations because $A_0,C_0$ are Kan, and all three comparison maps are weak equivalences. The strict pullbacks and their induced map are exactly the displayed squares and $v$.

source.place: Lemma 13.9, printed p. 31: 'i* is a homotopy monomorphism ... whence j* is a weak equivalence'; homotopy monomorphism in the sense of Section 12.2 (weak equivalence onto a union of components), expanded through the fiberwise Kan-fibration criterion.

proof.text: Form the strict pullback $Q=A_0^2\times_{C_0^2,v,\partial_C}C_1$. Its projection $q:Q\to C_1$ is the pullback of the weak equivalence $v$ along the Kan fibration $\partial_C$, hence is a weak equivalence by right properness. Endpoint commutation defines $u=(\partial_A,r_1'):A_1\to Q$ and gives $qu=r_1'$. Two-out-of-three makes $u$ a weak equivalence. The other projection $Q\to A_0^2$ is a Kan fibration: a horn lifting problem is a lifting problem for $\partial_C$ with its prescribed $A_0^2$ coordinate retained.

source.place: Lemma 13.9, printed p. 31: 'i* is a homotopy monomorphism ... whence j* is a weak equivalence'; homotopy monomorphism in the sense of Section 12.2 (weak equivalence onto a union of components), expanded through the fiberwise Kan-fibration criterion.

proof.text: Apply [lem-coef-kan-fibration-arbitrary-base-fibers] to $u$ over $A_0^2$: the structure map of $A_1$ is the endpoint Kan fibration from step 1 and that of $Q$ is the Kan fibration from step 8. The theorem gives a weak equivalence on their strict fibers over $b$. The first fiber is $M_A(jx,jy)$. The second is $D$: a simplex of the fiber is a pair $(b,\gamma)$ with $\partial_C\gamma=v(b)=c$, so forgetting its first coordinate and inserting that constant coordinate are inverse simplicial maps. Under these coordinates $u_b$ is exactly $T$ with target restricted to $D$. Thus $T$ factors as a weak equivalence to $D$ followed by inclusion of a union of components, including when those fibers are empty.

source.place: Lemma 13.9, printed p. 31: 'i* is a homotopy monomorphism ... whence j* is a weak equivalence'; homotopy monomorphism in the sense of Section 12.2 (weak equivalence onto a union of components), expanded through the fiberwise Kan-fibration criterion.

proof.text: Step 5 shows that $TJ$ is a weak equivalence, so it is surjective on components. Then $T$ is surjective on components too: for a component of $M_B(s_0x,s_0y)$, take a preimage component under $TJ$ and apply $J$. By steps 6–9, $T$ lands in the union of components $M_B(s_0x,s_0y)\cap C_1$. That union therefore meets every component of $M_B(s_0x,s_0y)$, so it is the whole space. Hence $T$ is itself a weak equivalence. Two-out-of-three for the Kan model structure, applied to $TJ$ and $T$, makes $J$ a weak equivalence. This holds for every pair $x,y$, including an empty mapping space: then $M_B(s_0x,s_0y)$ is empty because $TJ$ is a weak equivalence, and so is $M_A(jx,jy)$ because $T$ is one.

source.place: Lemma 13.9, conclusion that j induces weak equivalences on all mapping spaces; the component argument in the homotopy-monomorphism cancellation.

proof.text: Step 2 and step 10 say exactly that $j$ is a Dwyer--Kan equivalence. Apply the existing two-out-of-six theorem to the three composable maps $1_W:W\to W$, $j:W\to A$, and $p_i:A\to W$. Their successive composites are $j$ and $p_i j=1_W$, both Dwyer--Kan equivalences (identity maps induce identity functors and identity mapping-space maps). The theorem gives that $p_i$ is a Dwyer--Kan equivalence, for $i=0,1$. Step 1 already supplies the asserted Segal condition on $W^E$.
